items.prompt: At roughly what depth does the deep sea begin?

options.label: About 200 metres
options.feedback: The depth at which sunlight fades away.

options.label: About 20 metres
options.feedback: A diver at that depth still has plenty of light.

options.label: About 2,000 metres
options.feedback: Darkness has been complete long before that.

options.label: About 6,000 metres
options.feedback: That is the abyssal plain, far deeper down.

items.ok_line: Two hundred metres, where the last usable light gives out.
items.ko_line: The boundary is drawn where sunlight stops being enough to live by.
items.exp_title: The line where the sun gives up
items.exp_text: The deep sea is defined as beginning around 200 metres, where light fades past the point of supporting photosynthesis. Below it nothing green can grow, so every living thing depends on food falling from above or on chemistry at the seabed. Since the average ocean is some 3,700 metres deep, around ninety per cent of the ocean's volume lies below that line, in permanent darkness.

items.prompt: How many deep-sea animals produce their own light?

options.label: The large majority
options.feedback: Around three quarters of the main groups surveyed.

options.label: Only a handful of species
options.feedback: It is the rule down there, not the exception.

options.label: About one in ten
options.feedback: That is closer to the figure for coastal waters.

options.label: Almost none below 1,000 m
options.feedback: The deeper it gets, the commoner light becomes.

items.ok_line: In the darkest place on Earth, making light is normal.
items.ko_line: In the open deep ocean it is not a curiosity — it is the standard equipment.
items.exp_text: Surveys of the open Pacific found roughly three quarters of the main groups of deep-sea animals capable of producing light, against about one fortieth of organisms in coastal waters. More than seven hundred genera of animals are known to include glowing species. Since the deep sea is by far the largest habitat on the planet, making your own light is the ordinary condition of life on Earth, and we are the odd ones out.

items.prompt: Why is nearly all deep-sea light blue?

options.label: Blue travels furthest through water
options.feedback: Red is absorbed within a few metres.

options.label: Blue is the cheapest to produce
options.feedback: Cost is not what settles the colour.

options.label: Blue frightens most predators
options.feedback: It is the colour most eyes down there can see.

options.label: Sea water turns the light blue
options.feedback: It leaves the animal already blue.

items.ok_line: In water, blue is the only colour that carries.
items.ko_line: Water removes the colours one by one. Which one survives longest?
items.exp_text: Water absorbs long wavelengths fast — red is gone within a few metres — while blue penetrates furthest. So blue-green is the only light worth producing at depth, and most deep-sea eyes have narrowed until they can see almost nothing else. There are exceptions: one worm, Tomopteris, glows yellow, and a few fish have gone further still.

items.prompt: What advantage does a dragonfish gain by shining red?

options.label: Nothing else can see the beam
options.feedback: A private searchlight, invisible to its prey.

options.label: Red frightens its rivals away
options.feedback: Its rivals cannot see red either.

options.label: Red carries further than blue
options.feedback: Red is absorbed fastest of all in water.

options.label: Red attracts prey towards it
options.feedback: The prey never sees the light at all.

items.ok_line: It hunts with a lamp nobody else can detect.
items.ko_line: Down there, almost no eye can see red. Turn that into an advantage.
items.exp_title: A searchlight only one animal can see
items.exp_text: Barbeled dragonfishes emit a red glow and — uniquely — can see it, thanks to a pigment they appear to obtain from chlorophyll in the tiny copepods they eat. Since red light is filtered out of the ocean and almost nothing down there has eyes for it, the fish sweeps a beam across prey that cannot tell it is being lit. It also lights up red-pigmented animals that believed themselves invisible.

options.label: Glowing below to erase your silhouette
options.feedback: The belly is lit to match the water above.

options.label: Flashing to blind an attacker
options.feedback: That is a defensive burst, a different tactic.

options.label: Lighting the seabed to find food
options.feedback: These animals hang in open water.

options.label: Two animals signalling in turn
options.feedback: It is camouflage, not conversation.

items.ok_line: You fill in your own shadow, and vanish.
items.ko_line: Looking up from below, prey is a dark shape against faint light. How would you hide that?
items.exp_text: A hunter below looks upward and sees anything above it as a dark silhouette against the last of the daylight. Many squid and fish answer by lining their undersides with light organs and tuning them to match the brightness overhead. The firefly squid does this so precisely that light sensors on its body measure the background and adjust the glow to match — including when a cloud passes far above.

items.prompt: Where does an anglerfish's light actually come from?

options.label: Bacteria living in its lure
options.feedback: The fish houses and feeds them for the glow.

options.label: A gland in the fish's own head
options.feedback: The fish itself produces no light.

options.label: Food it has swallowed
options.feedback: Digested prey stops glowing.

options.label: Minerals in the water
options.feedback: Sea water gives off no light.

items.ok_line: It does not make the light. It keeps something that does.
items.ko_line: The fish is a landlord rather than a lamp.
items.exp_text: The bulb at the tip of an anglerfish's lure houses colonies of luminous bacteria, which the fish shelters and feeds in exchange for their glow. The arrangement is common in the sea: most luminous bacteria live free, but a great many have settled into partnerships with fish, squid and crustaceans. Some hosts have evolved organs shaped for one particular strain and can no longer glow without it.

items.prompt: Which is the most abundant fish of the deep sea?

options.label: The lanternfish
options.feedback: Small, glowing, and present in colossal numbers.

options.label: The anglerfish
options.feedback: Famous, but nothing like as numerous.

options.label: The viperfish
options.feedback: A striking hunter, and comparatively rare.

options.label: The cookiecutter shark
options.feedback: Small and widespread, but far behind.

items.ok_line: The commonest fish down there, and one of the commonest anywhere.
items.ko_line: The answer is a small fish covered in light organs, not one of the famous monsters.
items.exp_title: The most numerous vertebrate nobody has seen
items.exp_text: Lanternfish are by far the most abundant fish of the deep sea, carrying rows of light organs along their flanks and belly. They rise towards the surface each night to feed and sink again by day — a movement so vast that early sonar operators mistook the returning echo for a false seabed that rose and fell with the hours. It is now called the deep scattering layer.

items.prompt: Why do deep-sea animals still have working eyes if no sunlight reaches them?

options.label: There is plenty of living light to see
options.feedback: Eyes are kept to read what other animals emit.

options.label: They are left over and no longer used
options.feedback: Useless eyes are lost within a few generations.

options.label: They detect warmth rather than light
options.feedback: Eyes register light; heat is sensed elsewhere.

options.label: They see the faint glow of the seabed
options.feedback: The seabed itself does not glow.

items.ok_line: The darkness is full of lamps, so eyes remain worth keeping.
items.ko_line: Cave fish lose their eyes entirely. Why has the deep sea not done the same?
items.exp_title: Eyes for a world lit by animals
items.exp_text: Eyes are costly, and in true darkness they are abandoned — cave fish across the world have lost theirs. That deep-sea animals keep large, sensitive eyes is itself the proof that there is something to see: the flashes, lures and glowing clouds their neighbours produce. The contrast is the argument. No light, no eyes; eyes kept, therefore light.

items.prompt: What do many deep-sea animals do every night?

options.label: They rise towards the surface to feed
options.feedback: Then sink again before daylight returns.

options.label: They settle on the seabed to rest
options.feedback: Most live in open water and never touch bottom.

options.label: They stop glowing to save energy
options.feedback: Night is when the glowing is most useful.

options.label: They descend deeper to escape the cold
options.feedback: The deep water is colder, not warmer.

items.ok_line: The largest movement of animals on the planet, and it happens twice a day.
items.ko_line: Food is at the surface, and hunters can see you there by day. When would you go up?
items.exp_text: Each evening, uncounted billions of animals climb hundreds of metres to feed in the richer surface water, and sink back before dawn to where hunters cannot see them. By sheer mass it is the largest migration on the planet, and it happens every single day. It also carries carbon downward: animals feed at the top and release it far below, which makes this daily commute part of how the ocean stores carbon.

options.label: Vast areas of ocean glowing steadily
options.feedback: Bacteria shining across thousands of square kilometres.

options.label: Water made white by fine sediment
options.feedback: That is turbidity, and it does not glow.

options.label: Foam left behind by storms
options.feedback: Foam is white by day and dark by night.

options.label: Ice crystals forming at the surface
options.feedback: The effect is seen in warm tropical water.

items.ok_line: An ocean that glows steadily, bright enough to see from orbit.
items.ko_line: Sailors described a sea shining like snow all the way to the horizon. What could do that?
items.exp_text: Sailors have reported for centuries a sea glowing steadily and evenly to the horizon, sometimes for several nights. Unlike the sparkle stirred up by a moving boat, milky seas need no disturbance and are caused by bioluminescent bacteria in colossal numbers. Satellites have since confirmed them, one event covering an area larger than many countries. They remain rare, and nobody has yet sampled a large one directly.
